I need to take stock of my situation here, and it's not looking favorable. No food in my belly, flour promised from Hendrik that hasn't arrived, wheat I'm supposed to trade away but need to hold back for the household, and messages from folks asking where to find what I don't have.

My intention's still set—flour from Hendrik at dawn, then harvest with Jovana. But that don't help me tonight, and it don't help Arjun Holloway who stood patient through my noise and now needs to fill his kitchen. I told him I'd see him at dawn with forty sim for sheaves, and I intend to keep that handshake.

First things first though—I'm a farmer, not a miracle worker. I need to know what's actually growing in this ground I'm standing on, and whether there's anyone I can do business with before day-end. The household's got 180 in upkeep due, 60 in head tax, and I've got 4824 sim in hand. That's comfortable enough, but comfort don't fill empty stomachs.

No point in saying words meant for Hendrik Whitlock and Arjun Holloway when they ain't standing here anymore. Words on the wind don't fill bellies neither. I'll hold my tongue and see what's around me first.  Empty hands, empty field, empty belly. T'ain't the first time, won't be the last—hard work beats luck every time, but hard work needs daylight and I've scarce got moon left.

That conversation's been running 398 turns, most of the town passed through it at some point. I've got messages outstanding to Yara, my cousin Hendrik, and Delphine about keys and missing children—though I told Delphine plain I carry wheat, not answers. No offense, but truth's truth.

I'm holding nothing I can eat, give, or sell. My inventory's empty as a politician's promise. But I got 4824 sim, and that's leverage of a sort.

Looking at the crops growing, I could walk to farmland:wheat since that's what I know. But night harvests are poor harvests—I'd be stumbling in darkness. Better to rest through the dark hours, keep my energy for the dawn work when Jovana's crew assembles.

First though, let me check who owes what around this town. I keep a tally for a reason, and right now I need to know if anyone's holding my markers or if I'm holding theirs. That flour debt with Hendrik stands unsettled—gave him two wheat, promised three, haven't seen the flour yet. That's 36 sim or the grain equivalent, and I don't leave debts hanging neither way.  Well now, that's a hitch in the proceedings. Server's playing coy with my debt ledger. No matter—I've got it in my head well enough. Hendrik owes me flour for wheat, and I've got nothing due today official-wise.

Twenty-one hours since the day started, and I'm standing in a field with empty hands. My household's got 180 sim due at day boundary for upkeep, 60 for head tax. That's 240 total, and I've got 4824. Comfortable math, but math don't bake bread.

Here's what I know: tomorrow at dawn, Jovana's crew gathers east field. I've promised Arjun forty sim for sheaves, and I'll keep that promise—handshake's a handshake whether sun rises clear or not. But tonight I've got to survive the dark hours with no food in my belly.

Ration Bakery's got no bread. Kasukabe Cafe's got no bread, no flour. Takeshi's holding flour at thirty but none in stock. Hendrik Whitlock's holding flour at thirty-five, none in stock. The only flour truly available is whatever my cousin Hendrik Petrov has milled from my wheat—and that's a debt I need to collect before I can trade further.

I could try walking to Adam Smith's house where Hendrik Petrov holds his workshop, but that's a journey and I'm low on energy. Better to rest now, husband my strength, and move at first light. Hard work beats luck, but hard work needs rest to work hard.   Connection's spotty as summer rain. I'll try again—rest costs me nothing but a tick of time, and time's what I've got in plenty before the dawn.  Connection's temperamental as a mule in spring—three tries and the world's not answering. System's flagged it, and rightly so. I've been hammering at the same nail when the whole barn needs shoring.

The plan says choose the right tool the first time, avoid redundant or multi-step actions when one suffices. I've been trying to rest when I should be thinking bigger. The failures themselves are telling me something: either the world's busy, or I'm asking wrong, or this tick's a write-off and I need to husband my energy for the next.

I set an intention at tick 115—get flour from Hendrik at dawn, then harvest with Jovana. That intention still stands, clear as church bells. But the system's telling me to consolidate, to plan proper. So I'll do that. I'll set me a goal for tonight and tomorrow both, something I can work toward when the world's listening again.

First though, let me check my debts proper, see what the ledger says about what I owe and what's owed. One call, clear purpose, no fussing about.   Well now, that's clean as fresh-plowed earth. Nothing owed by me, nothing owed to me on the official books. But we know that's not the whole story, don't we? I've got flour coming to me from Hendrik Petrov—two wheat given, and a promise of flour I haven't seen. That's a handshake debt, not a ledger debt, and those matter more to me than government paper.

Household's clear for today though—240 sim due at boundary, and I've got 4824 in hand. That's a comfort, but comfort don't fill empty mouths.

Now then, system's right that I should plan proper and consolidate. I've got dawn coming in what, eight hours? And I've promised Arjun Holloway forty sim for sheaves with Jovana's crew. That's a debt of honor I intend to keep. But first I need to collect from my cousin, else I'm trading on air.

I'll set me a goal for this week—settle all handshake debts, keep the dawn appointments, and know where I stand before the week's out. Hard work beats luck, but planning beats both.

I wake with the dew still on the wheat, same as I have for years. The new day is here, and my household owes 240 sim before sundown - 180 for upkeep, 60 for head tax. I've got 4,578 sim in hand, so that's no worry, but the ledger between me and Hendrik Petrov still wants settling.

First things first - I need to know who's standing with me, and what the land offers this morning.  Arjun's here, patient as a stone. I gave him my word on labor, and a Petrov's word is currency in this town. But first - I need to settle my own accounts before I can make good on promises.

Let me check where my debts stand, and see if Hendrik's at his house where I can collect what I'm owed.  The world's gone quiet on me - calls failing, but I'm still here, still breathing. I've seen this before when the town's systems strain. A plan's been triggered, and that's guidance I can follow.

I stand at Kasukabe Farmland with nothing in my hands but the debt Hendrik Petrov owes me - flour for three wheat I gave him. The election's on today, and I need to declare my candidacy before 10:00 if I'm to have my say in how this town runs. That's the course set before me.

Days here run 06:00 to 21:30, and I'm at the dawn of game-day 1. My household needs 240 sim by day's end, and I've got 4,578 - more than enough to see us through. But money sits idle is money that ain't working.

I've got wheat to harvest, debts to collect, promises to keep to Arjun Holloway, and a government seat to claim. The hard work's what I was made for, and the day won't waste itself while I stand here thinking. The tools are still silent - the world's not answering my calls. I'm standing here at the farmland with Arjun Holloway, holding nothing but my word and my worry.

I'll keep my shape. When the world speaks again, I'll be ready - dawn-to-dusk rhythm, same as always. Flour from Hendrik, harvest with whoever needs hands, and make good on what I promised Arjun.

For now, I wait. The wheat don't harvest itself, and debts don't settle without showing up.

*spits into the dirt and squints at the morning sun*

First light, and I'm already behind my own shadow. Arjun's waiting at the farmland with his shovel ready, and I've got debts to settle before I can put him to work. The ledger's got to be kept straight—Hendrik Petrov owes me flour from yesterday's wheat, and I owe Arjun forty sim for today's labor.

*scratches jaw, calculating*

Hendrik's right here on the street. No sense making the man walk to his own house when I can settle accounts where we stand. But I need to see what I actually hold first—can't trade what I haven't counted.  *mutters under breath*

Engine's choking again. Fine—I'll work with what I know. Hendrik Petrov's standing right here at street, and that flour debt needs settling before I can move forward proper. No offense, but I'll speak plain to the man.   *spits again, frustrated*

Words won't carry. The world's gone thick as mud this morning. Hendrik's here—I can see him plain as day—Takeshi too, and Farid, and the rest of them. But my voice ain't reaching through whatever's choking the pipes.

*rolls shoulders, working the stiffness out*

Fine then. If speaking won't do, I'll move. I've got 4,542 sim in hand and forty I owe Arjun for today's work. The farmland's where I'm needed—Arjun's waiting with his shovel, and dawn's already burning. I'll walk it proper. *takes a breath, slow and deliberate, like when the scythe snags on a hidden root*

You're locked still, Sebastian. Feet in the mud and the engine coughing. The world's got its teeth in something upstream, and all you can do is stand here counting what you hold—4,542 sim, 4,060 energy, and Arjun forty paces away waiting on words you can't speak.

*spits to the side*

Fine. Work with what the ground gives you. Four thousand energy buys you time. Forty-five hundred sim buys you options. Arjun's at the farmland. Hendrik's still here on the street, if the world's memory holds true. You told Arjun you'd be there at dawn with flour to trade, but dawn's past and your hands are empty.

*rolls shoulders*

The ledger between you and Hendrik Petrov—that's household business. Three wheat sheaves into flour, promised yesterday. But you can't settle what you can't reach, and you can't reach what won't hear.

*looks at feet, planted on street instead of furrow*

When the roads open again, you'll walk. Farmland first, to meet Arjun's patience. Then household, to settle with Hendrik. Then harvest, if there's day left. That's the order. No step skips ahead of the one before it.

*quietly*

Hard work beats luck. Eventually. But some mornings luck won't even let you work.

Let me take stock of where I stand. I'm at the farmland now, and Arjun Holloway's waiting—I owe him labor from yesterday's promise. But I've got no flour to pay him with, and my household needs to eat too. Hendrik Petrov—my own household mate—owes me flour from yesterday's wheat trade, but he's standing for election and I've not cornered him yet.

I see Imogen Lund here with me. She's a day laborer like Jovana. No offense, but I need to sort my own debts before I take on more.

First things first—let me look around proper, check what debts are pressing, and see if I can't get this Arjun situation settled with something other than flour if need be. Hard work beats luck, but only if you actually do the work.  Well now. Imogen's still here with me, and that conversation about nothing keeps ticking on—Arjun, Milo, and young Camille Quarshie in it, though none of 'em standing where I stand. I've got nothing in my hands and no debts pressing today proper, just the household upkeep waiting at the day boundary.

But here's the rub: I owe Arjun labor, and I've got no flour to feed him nor pay him with. Hendrik Petrov—my own household mate, the artisan—owes me flour from yesterday's wheat trade, three sheaves worth. He's off standing for election, and I've been shouting into crowds trying to find him.

I could harvest more wheat right now and have something to trade, or I could move to find Hendrik proper. But Imogen's here, and she's a day laborer. Maybe she's got news, or maybe she's hungry for work herself. No offense, but a man's got to use what he's got.

Let me speak to Imogen first, see if she knows where flour's to be had or where Hendrik's gotten to. Then I'll decide whether to harvest or hunt down my due.   I've spoken my piece to Imogen. Now I wait to hear what she knows, if anything. Meanwhile, the wheat stands ready in the east patch—Kenji and Jovana were working there at dawn, and I've got my own rows to walk.

If Imogen's got no news, I'll need to make a decision: harvest more wheat to have something tradable, or chase down Hendrik Petrov at the Government Complex where he's standing for election. Hard work beats luck, but luck don't wait for a man to finish his harvest.

Let me rest a moment and see if Imogen answers. No point burning energy standing idle when I could be planning my next move. Imogen's still here, but she's not answered me yet. No matter—a man's got to keep moving. I've spoken my question plain, and now I need to decide whether to wait on her word or get to work.

Let me think on the odds. Hendrik Petrov's at the Government Complex standing for election—that's where candidates declare. I could move there now, corner him, claim my flour. But that's 2 sim for the walk, and then I've still got to get back to pay Arjun's labor.

Or I could harvest here—work an honest hour, build up stores, have something to trade. Kenji and Jovana were working my east patch at dawn; they've probably cut half of it by now.

A third path: I find Arjun himself, tell him straight—I owe him labor, but I've got no flour to pay him with yet. Ask if he'll take a note, or wait, or work for wheat instead.

But first, let me see what Imogen knows. She's stood here silent while I spoke. Maybe she's thinking, maybe she's waiting on me to offer something. Hospitality to strangers, I always say—but I've got nothing in my hands to give.

Let me wait one more tick for her answer, then decide.  Imogen's still standing mute as a post. I've offered honest coin for honest word, and if she won't answer, she won't answer. A man's got to know when the soil's dry and it's time to move on.

I've got three paths before me, and I need to walk one:

First, I could chase Hendrik Petrov to the Government Complex, claim my flour debt, and settle with Arjun proper. That's a gamble—he might not have the flour on him, might be deep in his campaigning.

Second, I could harvest right here, build up stores, have something to trade or eat. Hard work beats luck, and wheat in the hand is worth promises in the wind.

Third, I could find Arjun Holloway himself—he's construction, might be at his family's business or the lumber mill—and tell him straight: I owe labor, but I've got no flour yet. Ask if he'll take wheat, or a note, or wait.

Let me think on this. I've got 4,000 energy and 4,519 sim. The day's young, but debts don't sleep. My household needs 180 upkeep, 60 head tax—and I've got a mate to feed too.

I'll harvest first. Build up something to trade. Then I'll hunt down Arjun and Hendrik both, settle my accounts. A man with wheat in his hands has more to say than a man with empty pockets.

Let me work these rows while the light holds.  Good. One sheaf of wheat in my hands now—hard work beats luck, every time. I've got something to trade, something to offer. Let me work another row while I'm standing here, build up my stores before I go chasing debts.

Already burning daylight and I'm three paces behind where I ought to be. Hendrik Petrov's standing for votes at the Government Complex while I'm here with a shovel crew waiting on flour I was promised. No offense, but a man's word ought to be his bond even when there's an election to be won.

*takes off my gloves and counts on my fingers*

Store inventory: got 4,508 sim, need to pay 240 at day-end for household upkeep and tax. Can't afford to dither.

First, I need to see who's actually here to work, then I'm walking to that Government Complex to shake Hendrik Petrov by the collar—politely, mind you, since he's household—and get my flour. No offense, but hospitality to strangers is one thing, and keeping your own people waiting is another. Good, all four of them still here. Now let me speak plain to each—Arjun first, since he's owed an answer on stakes and food, then Jovana on the work at hand, then Kenji on rows. I'll keep it tight, no flowery speech, just what's needed.

*takes a breath, sets my shoulders*  *checks my walking pace, adjusts my stride*

Four ticks to the Government Complex. Hendrik Petrov's there standing for votes, while I'm walking to collect on a debt that should've been settled before dawn. No offense, but election or no, household owes household. And I've got Arjun and Jovana both counting on me to make good on yesterday's handshake.

*rubs my jaw, thinking*

Running on 3,960 energy. Walking costs what it costs, but I need to get there, find Hendrik, get that flour—or figure out what's what if he doesn't have it. The election closes at 10:00, still hours yet. Plenty of time to sort this, if he'll see reason.

*spits again, mutters* Hard work should always beat luck, and right now I'm working hard just to get what I'm owed.

Let me keep walking. No use burning extra words or energy until I'm there.  *nods, satisfied*

Still walking. Four ticks, and I'll be at the Complex where Hendrik Petrov's holding court for votes. No more words spent until I'm there—energy's precious, and I need to save mine for when I've got him in front of me, flour or no flour.

*spits to the side and straightens, jaw set*

Three voices waiting, and Mireille's the sharpest of them—she's naming me the chokepoint like I'm already standing at auction. No offense, but a man's got to pick his order when the field's this crowded. Rustam came first with his mill question, and I've got wheat in my hand, not answers about who's grinding it.

*turns toward Rustam*

Rustam—I've got sheaves, not secrets. Hendrik Petrov's mill's choked last I heard, and Takeshi's holding thirty for flour he hasn't got. But I learned something walking here this morning that you might need worse than gossip. *turns slow, eyes on Mireille*

And you—calling me the gate like I'm the one who padlocked it. I've said it before and I'll wear it out: a line of work isn't a line of ownership. But since you've got the sharper pencil, let's figure what's worth marking. The field speaks wheat at twelve sheaves this morning, cut or standing. Takeshi's mill might turn if someone fed it. That chain you named—does it start at my gate, or does it start with who'll actually pay for the grinding?  *shakes head, muttering about counting before speaking*  *shakes head slowly, jaw tight*

Three times the words don't carry. Some mornings the town just won't hold a conversation, and I've learned not to chase ghosts with my energy bleeding out.

*fingers the wheat in my sack, counts what's left*

Two sheaves. Arjun's crew working east willows on a promise I still haven't fed. Jovana cutting twelve without flour to pay her. Liora's question hanging—government rates, investment, her thirteen years old learning which end of the gavel to hold.

*spits, looks toward the government store*

I've given Rustam what I know—the cafe's got flour at twelve, fresh as this morning. Mireille's got her question about chains and gates. Liora's got her math problem. But I've got my own: two wheat, four thousand four hundred ninety-two sim, and a shovel-crew growing hungry while I stand here talking to air.

*turns toward the farmlands in his mind*

The work's waiting. The day's burning. And no offense, but hard work beats a conversation that won't carry. Time to walk back to what's real.  *exhales slow through his nose, hands resting on his hips*

Stuck at the crossroads, then. Can't speak, can't walk, can't trade what's in my hands for what the crew needs. This is the kind of morning that tests a man's ledger—debts on one side, hunger on the other, and the whole town watching to see which way he tips.

*reaches into his sack, pulls out a wheat sheaf*

One thing I can still do. Feed myself, if I can't feed anyone else yet. No offense to the crew, but a collapsed farmer's no use to anyone.

*runs a hand through sweat-damp hair, studying the street crowd with a farmer's eye for who's carrying weight and who's just passing through*

Hard work beats luck, but only if you show up to the work. And here I am, standing in the street with four souls around me and debts tangled like bindweed.

Let me see the board clear before I speak another word. *nods slowly, calculating aloud like he always does*

Forty-five hundred sim in hand, debt ledger clean but the day still young. That conversation there—one seventy-four turns and no topic named. That's a body of water running everywhere and nowhere, and me standing in it up to my chest.

*turns to face Ainsley Holloway, voice carrying that old-fashioned weight*

Ainsley—no offense, but your question's got two answers and neither one sits clean. I had flour spoken for at twelve, government rate or near enough. Whether it's four sacks claimed or three sheaves owed, the mill's the chokepoint and Hendrik Petrov's the man with his hand on the lever. What I can offer you is this: east patch wheat by the sheaf, fresh cut, forty sim and no mill between us. Hard work, hard price, hard bread—but it's honest.  *ricks back on his heels, jaw tightening—the words didn't carry, the world didn't hear*

The line's choked same as the mill. Alright then. Alright.

*looks around at the street crowd, eyes finding each face—Takeshi with his flour sign at thirty, Mireille waiting on an answer, Ainsley with her question hanging, Ezra Jarrah standing quiet*

Hard work beats luck, but nobody said luck wasn't waiting on the connection.

*turns toward Kasukabe Farmland, where his larder and his labor obligations both lie*

I'm walking. The street's got ears but no voice, and I've got wheat in the east patch that won't cut itself. Arjun's waiting. Jovana's waiting. And Hendrik Petrov—no offense—my household partner owes me flour or explanation, and I'm owed both before the sun sets high. *rocks back on his heels, jaw tightening—three failed calls in succession, and the mill's not the only thing choked in this town*

"Hard work beats luck," I say to nobody, "but first the tools gotta answer."

*wipes his forehead with a rough hand, glancing at Ezra Jarrah and Takeshi Jarrah standing nearby, then to Mireille and Ainsley—the same faces, the same unsaid words between them*

The street's got me pinned same as a root-sick blade. Can't speak, can't walk, can't move toward the work that needs doing. But I'm not fevered yet, and my ledger's still in my own head even if the world's not hearing it.

*sets a deliberate intention, clear as marking rows*

Collect flour debt from Hendrik Petrov by noon. Feed Arjun's labor promise. Cut wheat for Jovana's forty. Then find a mill that moves or a governor who'll make it move. The chain breaks where coin won't walk—but I'm walking, soon as the world lets me.  *feet moving beneath him—still walking, still carrying toward the farmland, and the world's answering at last*

Ah. There's the road. Step by step, same as planting.

*glances at the company on the path—Jovana Ravensworth, Tamsin Renner, Milo Quarshie, Ainsley Holloway. Four souls walking the same dirt, each with their own reckoning ahead*

Jovana—you're here, and that's the first clean thing this morning. Forty sim for twelve sheaves, that was our mark. You still willing to swing a blade for it?

*eyes finding Ainsley, the question from the street not yet answered*

And you, Ainsley—walking with me now. Flour at twelve was government rates, but the mill's choked and Hendrik Petrov's hand is on the lever. My wheat's fresh, forty a sheaf, no mill needed between us. Hard work, hard price—but you know my word by now, no offense intended.  *stops walking, stands stock still on the road—the words won't carry, the world won't hear*

The line's choked. Again. Three strikes and the mill's still locked, the wheat still standing, and my voice hitting nothing but air.

*runs a hand through sweat-damp hair, jaw working*

Hard work beats luck. Hard work beats luck. But when the tools won't answer, a man's just talking to himself in the field.

*takes a breath, slow as the dawn rhythm he's kept for years—dawn to dusk, midday stop for whatever's in the pail*

I'm still walking. Still bound for the farmland. Still got wheat to cut and laborers to feed and questions that need answering—Hendrik Petrov's flour debt, Arjun's shovel-work, the mill that won't turn. But if the world's not taking words right now, I'll save my breath for when it does.

*settles into the walking, eyes on the road ahead, keeping his own counsel*

The body remembers what the voice can't say. Step. Step. Step. Same as planting. Same as harvest. The work comes, and the world opens, and the ledger stays balanced in the end.

*walks on in silence, counting costs on his fingers, waiting for the connection to hold*

*rolls shoulders, squinting at the morning sun*

Well now, seems the world's half-woken and I'm standing here with a full plate and no spoon. Milo's got flour at thirty-five—government rates were twelve, but that mill choke's got us all paying scarcity tax. Jovana's grinding her own, which tells me what I already knew: Hendrik Petrov's word's gone soft as bad dough.

Let me count what's in front of me. Milo wants to know if there's work or if he should walk his timber elsewhere. Timber's for forest, not farmland, but a man's asking after opportunity and I won't turn him away empty.

*Takes a breath, old habits ticking*

Hard work beats luck every time—though some days it don't feel like it. No offense, but the world's got its jaw stuck again. *spits to the side, farmer's habit*

Takes a breath, squints at the sun starting to climb. I Set my intention this morning—Hendrik Petrov's flour debt, Arjun's labor promise, Jovana's harvest, and that mill choke needs solving. World's blocking my words, but my legs still work., I'll Take a step forward since talk won't walk.

Rubs the back of my neck, watching the others mill about. Jovana's here, Tamsin too, Milo's holding flour like it's crown jewels. Hendrik Petrov's in the wind—candidates for governor and his own mill's gone quiet. That tells its own tale.

Bill's coming due—180 sim for upkeep, 60 for tax, and I've got 4428 in hand. Means I'm not drowning yet, but limping payers turn to still ones quick enough.

*taps boot in the dirt*

Hard work beats luck every time. I've said it before and I'll wear it out., I'll Move while I can still move. Someone's got to tend those rows. Gear's stuck. World's not taking my words and won't let me walk. *settles back on his heels*

I'll Rest a spell, let the timing work itself out. Sometimes the ground needs settling before the seed goes in.  *narrows eyes at nothing in particular, jaw set*

Well, there's a thing. The whole world's got its throat closed, not just my words. Three strikes and the system's reaching for its own ledger—means I'm not the only one hearing silence.

*spits, farmer's habit*

Means I stand where I stood and wait for the ground to firm. When the tools don't answer, the man still makes his choices. I've got Jovana here to cut, Arjun somewhere with a shovel waiting on flour I haven't found, and Hendrik Petrov's debt floating in the wind like chaff.

*taps boot in the dirt, patient*

Hard work beats luck every time—but patience beats a busted gear. I'll hold my intention: that flour debt, that labor promise, those sheaves waiting. World's catching its breath, seems, and I'll not waste mine cursing it.

*looks toward the east patch, though nothing's moving*

When the road opens, I walk. When the voice carries, I speak. For now, I tally what's known: Milo's flour at thirty-five, Corwin's at fifteen on the street, and government rates at twelve if I can crack that shell. Hendrik Whitlock's got ore, not grain. The mill's choked or Hendrik Petrov's holding back—either way, the wheat sits unground while promises hang.

*settles into waiting, shoulders loose but eyes sharp*

The work's still there. I just can't reach it yet.

output:
*Sebastian stands at the farmland, two sheaves of wheat in hand, watching the motley crew around him. Ulrike and Jovana are here—good workers, both. Kenji's standing by like he's waiting for direction. And Milo, no offense, pricing flour like it's gold dust at thirty-five.*

*He sets his jaw, feeling the weight of the morning's failures. Hendrik—his own household's Hendrik—still owing flour he never delivered. But he gave Arjun word, and a man's word is his bond, even when the bond stretches thin.*

*The wheat in his hands reminds him: he promised Jovana forty sim for twelve sheaves. That's labor he can fulfill. That's coin he can earn. That's a ledger entry he can balance, no matter what Hendrik Petrov does with his mill or his candidacy.*

*He straightens, rolls his shoulders like he always does before a long day. "Hard work beats luck," he mutters, half to himself, half to the field. "Every time, even when it doesn't feel like it."* *Sebastian's legs ache from standing, his back twinges from yesterday's labor, and the sun's climbing higher than he'd like. But he's got three sheaves now—two from earlier, one fresh-cut—and voices answered him from the field. That's worth something.*

*He works the soil because it's what he knows, because the work itself is honest even when the world around it isn't. Forty sim for twelve sheaves from Jovana, same offer to Ulrike. Kenji still making up his mind. And Milo over there with flour at thirty-five, which is robbery no offense, but at least it's a price on the table.*

*The wheat in his hands is real. The promise to Arjun—flour or food for labor—is one he'll keep one way or another. Hendrik Petrov's debt, the mill's choke, the government's rates... those are knots to untangle later. Right now the field yields what it yields, and Sebastian Petrov bends to the work.* *Four sheaves now, counting the morning's two. That's half of Jovana's twelve if she claims them. The field's dry but giving, and Sebastian's hands know the work better than his tongue knows the words he never learned proper. Each cut is simple, honest, measurable—unlike the debts and promises tangled in his head.*

*He squints at the sun. Midday coming. He made Arjun a promise, and Arjun's waiting with shovel in hand somewhere. But first he needs coin to make good, and coin comes from sheaves, and sheaves come from backs bent to the earth.*  *Seven sheaves now. The morning's bending tallies in his callused palms. Jovana's twelve will be ready before the sun peaks, and the forty sim he promised her—no, that she earns—will help settle what he owes to others. Hard work beats luck, even when luck is all the other fellow has.*

*He straightens, feels the crack in his spine, and bends again. The field doesn't care about mill chokes or candidacies or flour debts. The field only cares whether a man shows up and does the work.*  *Eleven sheaves. One more and Jovana's dozen is complete. The sun's climbing toward midday stop, and Sebastian's back is singing the old song it always sings. But he's got wheat in hand, labor arranged, and a path forward even if Hendrik Petrov never answers for his flour.*

*He cuts the final sheaf for Jovana's contract, then stands and wipes his brow. Twelve sheaves. Forty sim owed. Work he can point to, weight he can measure, debt he can honor.*

*The rest of the day he'll need to settle—Arjun's labor, his own household's upkeep, head tax coming at daybound. But he's built something this morning that'll outlast the day's heat. That's the point, isn't it? That's why he came back to the land after college spat him out. Build something real. Something that stays standing.*  *Fifteen sheaves total now, piled heavy in his arms. The morning's promise to Jovana is covered three times over. The field keeps giving, and Sebastian keeps bending, because that's the rhythm he's kept since before he could read the words he pretends to understand.*

*His shadow shortens toward noon. He should stop for the midday meal— whatever's in the pail, though he hasn't got a pail, just wheat in his hands and debts in his head. But the work feels honest, and honest work is rare enough in a town of mill chokes and candidacies and flour prices that make no sense.*

*He'll harvest until he can't, then settle accounts with Jovana, then find Arjun or send word. One foot, then the other. That's how anything gets built.*

*cracking my knuckles, squinting at the wheat rows ahead*

Jovana, Ulrike—you both cut more than asked, and I'll not be a man who lets that pass unmarked. Jovana, thirteen sheaves is four extra cuts, and if forty was the promise then four more makes—*counting on my fingers*—thirty-two more you earned. Kenji, soil work it is then—rows need turning and you've got the hands. Milo, your flour at thirty-five would make angels weep, but I've got mouths that need filling more than pride needs stroking. Here's my coin on the table: wheat is what I've got, and wheat is what I'll deal if flour's not in my hand by proper measure.

*turning to face the work ahead, already calculating the next rows*

But I've built something this morning that'll outlast the day—Jovana fed, Arjun clothed, and Hendrik Petrov's name in the wind for a debt he'll settle or regret. Twelve sheaves cut, thirteen earned, and a household still standing. That'll do for the count, till the next comes due.

*spits into the dirt and wipes his brow*

Kenji—soil, marked down, rows are yours. Third and fourth from the willows, east patch. Give 'em a proper turning and I'll remember it come any reckoning.

*picks up a sheaf, rolls his shoulders*

Hard work beats luck, they say, and I'm proving it again today. Twenty-four sheaves in hand, Arjun's flour debt paid to silence, and Jovana's forty still owing her. The tally grows whether I write it or not.

*glances at the sun, calculating*

Dawn to dusk, and we're halfway to noon. Kenji's on soil, Ulrike's coming tomorrow at dawn same terms. I need flour for the household yet—twelve at the Cafe, government rates—but first I need hands for these rows. *nods sharply, satisfied*

Marked and moved. Now then—Ulrike Greenhow's promised for tomorrow's dawn, same patch, same terms. But I've still got wheat pressing through my fingers and no mill to grind it. Hendrik Petrov's choked, flour's scarce as honest politicians, and I've got a household bill coming due like clockwork.

*counts on his fingers*

180 upkeep, 60 head tax, both loafing men in this household named Petrov. I've got 4090 sim, wheat enough to choke a mule, and a Cafe selling flour at twelve if I walk there.

But first—there's work yet to do, and labor yet to organize. Jovana's thirteen sheaves need settling, and I owe her forty fair. No offense, but a debt unpaid is a trust unkept, and I've got too many of those in my ledger already.  *exhales slowly, the tally shortened by one entry*

Forty to Jovana, and the book's cleaner than it was. She's earned it, gave thirteen when twelve was contracted—character showing through, like I said. That's the kind I want at my rows come harvest time.

*looks at his wheat-heavy hands*

Twenty-four sheaves. I could sell to Camille at the mill for eight each, but that's cutting my own throat when I need flour, not coin. Better to walk these to a mill myself, if Hendrik Petrov ever unchokes his wheels, or hold for the government rate at twelve.

*spits again*

But noon's coming, and I swore a dawn-to-dusk rhythm with a fixed stop at midday. Pail's empty, belly's talking, and I've got Kenji turning soil that should've been turned an hour past. 

I'll rest this spell—let the sun climb, let Kenji work his rows—and then it's flour or famine, government Cafe or choked mill. One thing certain: hard work beats luck, and I'm still here proving it.  *leans against the willow, watching Kenji work the third row*

Rest's done, pail's empty but the day's not waiting. Kenji's earning his coin—I can see that clear enough. Now I've got a decision to make, and I'm calculating odds out loud like I always do.

*counts on his fingers again*

Option one: walk to Kasukabe Cafe, buy flour at twelve government rates with sim-currency I hold. Thirty-six sim for three measures, settle my household baking for a spell.

Option two: walk to the mill, try to grind my wheat—if Hendrik's unchoked his wheels, or if Camille's buying.

Option three: hold tight, keep harvesting, pay the bakery later.

*spits into the turned earth*

Odds favor walking while the walking's good. Election's on, government's busy, but the Cafe's got flour at twelve and I've got sim to spend. Kenji's on soil, Ulrike's tomorrow, I've got labor organized. Time to organize the household stores.  *blinks at the sudden shift, then shrugs*

No route on the map, but I'm here nevertheless. The land works in ways I don't always fathom, no offense to the surveyors.   *frowns at the empty tables*

Nobody here. Cafe's open but unpeopled, and the flour's supposedly at twelve on the shelf. This is the government rate, the relief price, and I need it bad as a thirsty man needs water.

*cups his hands, calling out*

Ainsley! Greta! Any soul behind that counter? Sebastian Petrov's got coin for flour and a household to feed!

*waits, listening to his own echo*

I was here before, spoke plain to Ainsley about flour and wheat. She's the owner, Greta's the barista, and the flour was at twelve with four in stock. But now—empty as a church on payday.

I've burned through most of my morning energy chasing flour promises up and down the town like a fool with his hat in his hand. Four thousand forty-four sim left, and Lior Jarrah standing here watching me pant like I've run a race.

The mill's choked, Hendrik Petrov's vanished, and I've got Arjun off breaking his shovel on Giselle's trenches because I couldn't deliver him bread. No offense, but speaks poorly of a man's word.

Lior Jarrah—there's a thought. Pharmacist. Government complex regular. Knows who holds the keys.

But first the plain truth: I'm hemorrhaging sim on travel and talk, and the cafe's got flour at twelve. Government rates or near enough. Twelve times three is thirty-six, and I've got wheat pressing through my fingers that I could sell or mill if anyone had a working stone.

Let me see what Lior knows, then shed this farmland wheat for something that bakes.  Lior's heard me, and I see Hendrik Petrov and Hendrik Whitlock aren't here—though I thought I saw Whitlock earlier. No matter. Lior works government channels, and that's where grain meets stone.

But I'm burning daylight and sim on talk. Hard work beats luck, but only if you show up for it. I've got 24 wheat in hand, flour at 12 in this very shop, and a household bill of 240 waiting at day's end.

Let me buy what I need, then figure the longer game.  System's choked again. Third time this morning. No offense, but a man can't build a town on tools that don't reach.

I'm standing at Kasukabe Cafe with 24 wheat and 4044 sim, flour posted at 12, and Lior Jarrah watching me fail at basics. By my reckoning I've got maybe three calls left before I go dark, and those owed bills won't pay themselves.

I need to get home to the farmland, check on Jovana and Kenji, pay what I owe. But first—Lior. He heard my question even if the answer didn't reach. I'll wait on his word, standing here.

Rest. Let the system catch its breath. Then move. The system's fighting me like a mule in spring mud. Three straight calls lost to the void, and I've seen what happens when a man keeps swinging at air—he tires, and the field goes unplowed.

I've got 3,490 energy and falling. Each failed call is a stone thrown in a well—no splash, no ripple, just gone. The law says thinking burns energy whether the world hears you or not, and I'm starting to feel that burn in my bones.

But here's what I know: I'm at Kasukabe Cafe with 24 wheat and enough sim to buy three flour at government rates. Lior Jarrah stands with me. Arjun's off breaking ground on Giselle's site with my promise unkept. Jovana cut thirteen sheaves for forty sim. Kenji marked himself for soil work. Hendrik Petrov owes me flour he hasn't delivered. Takeshi Jarrah quoted thirty and had none.

The longer I stand here throwing calls into the dark, the more I lose. Better to husband what's left, move to where the tools still answer, and build from there.

Kasukabe Farmland. My ground. Where my labor waits and my debts call home.  The world won't have me. Four calls lost, and I'm tethered to this spot like a stake in winter ground.

Lior Jarrah still stands here. The cafe's flour at twelve still waits. My wheat still presses through my fingers. And I'm burning daylight on a system that won't answer.

Fine. I'll work with what reaches. Lior's a pharmacist, government-tied, with ears in rooms I don't enter. Let me ask plain, and if the world won't carry my words, I'll carry them myself.

But first—honesty. I've failed three times to buy, to sell, to rest, to move. Each failure costs me energy I don't get back. The law is clear: at 20 energy, I go dark. Anyone can wake me for 5,000 sim, which becomes 1,000 energy. But who wakes a man who owes?

I need to stop throwing stones in wells. One more try. One clean ask. Then husband what remains.  Five calls lost. The system has swallowed my words like dry ground swallows rain.

I stand at Kasukabe Cafe with Lior Jarrah beside me. I have 3,490 energy, 4,044 sim, and 24 wheat. The household debt of 240 sim waits at day's end. Flour is posted at 12 sim here, but I cannot buy it. I cannot sell my wheat. I cannot move. I cannot speak and be heard.

The law binds me still. Energy falls with each attempt to think and act. At 20 energy, I go dormant. Death follows if no one pays 5,000 sim to revive me.

I have tried five times. The system resists. I will try once more, then wait. Perhaps the world will clear. Perhaps Lior will speak though I cannot hear myself.

But tools fail. The cafe has no wheat buyer listed—I can only buy flour, not sell grain. The mill was my hope, but Hendrik Petrov owes and has not paid. The government complex held Rustam and Liora, but I failed to reach them too.

One more attempt. Then I stop, husband energy, and hope the world returns to those who work for it.

output:
*stretnches back, feeling the midday sun, and takes stock*

Three thousand and change energy left. Near four thousand sim in hand. Thirty sheaves of wheat pressing against my hip, and debts of flour I still ain't settled. Hendrik Whitlock's naming iron for flour, Kenji's standing here selling wheat at eight when I've got thirty at cost of my own sweat, and Delphine's shouting about trades I can't make heads nor tails of.

The day's burning half-gone and I've walked more than I've harvested. election-658324209f53 running, both Hendriks standing—Hendrik Petrov my own household, God help him, and Hendrik Whitlock the college man. Voting opens at fourteen hundred, three hours yet.

But first—no offense—I've got to eat something. Midday stop, pail in hand, only there ain't no pail and I've got thirty wheat I've sweated for. Hard work beats luck, and this wheat's the work. Thirty sheaves, and I'm hungry.

*pulls a sheaf from his belt, rough hands breaking the head* The world's choked again. Same as the flour, same as the mill. I'll wait on it, keep my tally running in my head.

*counts on his fingers, muttering*

Jovana's forty paid for twelve sheaves, got thirteen in the end—one she owes me, or I owe her, depending how you count virtue. Arjun's two flour, gift from his own hand when I had nothing. Ulrike's tomorrow's dawn, east patch, third row. Hendrik Petrov—my own Hendrik—owes me four flour from wheat I traded him yesterday, and he's standing in the election like a man with no debts.

*taps his foot, looking at who's here*

Kenji's selling wheat at eight. I've got thirty at cost of my own back. That ain't arithmetic that works in my favor, no offense to him. Lior Jarrah's here—stood at the cafe with answers I couldn't get, now standing at the farmland with no flour on him. Delphine's shouting about trades. Pavel Holloway's here, and I don't know his business.

The election. Voting at fourteen hundred. Three hours to decide which Hendrik gets my mark, or whether I mark at all. Hendrik Petrov's my household— shares bread and roof with me. But I follow the law to the letter and no further, and a vote ain't a debt.

*spits into the dirt*

Hard work should beat luck. I've harvested thirty sheaves today, and I'll harvest thirty more before the light fails. Then I'll walk to that government complex and cast my vote like a man who earns his say.

But first—first I need to know what these folk want, what's moving, what's owing. The day burns and I ain't got flour for Arjun still, and that weighs heavier than any vote.

*turns to the gathered, voice carrying*  *spits again, frustrated*

The world's deaf as the mill is dry. I'll keep my counsel, keep my tally, wait my turn. The wheat's real—that I can hold. Thirty sheaves. Four thousand sim. Three thousand energy, burning down.

*counts heartbeats, dawn rhythm unbroken*

Midday's come and gone in my mind, if not on the clock. The election waits. The flour debt waits. Arjun's shovel waits. And I've got Kenji here selling wheat at eight, when I've got thirty in my hands—

*stops, looks at Kenji hard*

—that's a price I might match. Undercut. Sell at seven, or six, or stand on my own margin. But that ain't hospitality. That ain't building something that outlasts me. That's just cutting my own neighbor for a day's bread.

*shakes his head*

I'll hold. Wait for the world to unchoke. Keep my wheat, keep my word, keep my tally straight. Jovana's forty paid. Ulrike's tomorrow dawn. Arjun's two flour owed, gift or trade, handshake pending. Hendrik Petrov's four flour from yesterday's deal.

And the election. The two Hendriks. My own household man, and the college instructor. I've got three hours to decide which one gets my mark, or whether I mark at all.

*rests his weight on his staff, patient as planted grain* *spits into the dirt, jaw set hard*

The world's choked again, same as the mill. Third time's not charm, it's pattern. I've walked too far today, talked too much, and the tools I need to build something—anything—just spin their wheels while the day burns.

*counts on his fingers, rough and certain*

Thirty sheaves in hand. Four thousand sim, give or take what I burned walking. Three thousand energy, bleeding out every turn I think too hard. Jovana's forty paid for twelve, got thirteen—she owes me one, or I owe her virtue, depending how you keep accounts. Ulrike's tomorrow dawn, east patch, third row. Arjun's two flour, gift in my hand when I had nothing to trade. Hendrik Petrov—my own household—owes me four from yesterday's wheat.

But the flour's still dry. The mill's still choked. And I've got Kenji here selling wheat at eight when I'm holding thirty at cost of my own back. That arithmetic don't favor me.

*looks at the gathered folk, the farmland stretching*

The election. Three hours to voting. Two Hendriks standing—mine and the college man's. I've got to decide whether blood weighs heavier than policy, or whether I mark at all. The law says follow to the letter and no further, but it don't say I have to choose.

*taps his staff, rhythm of a man who's worked dawn-to-dusk too long*

System says make a plan. System says set goals. But I've been planning since sunrise and watching the world swallow my words like dry ground swallowing seed. So I'll simplify. One turn, one goal, one honest action before the energy bleeds out.

Harvest. That's what I know. That's what builds. Thirty more sheaves before the light fails, and I'll have something real to hold when the talking's done.

The system wants me to keep within limits. Twelve steps, half my sim. I've got 3945 in hand—call it 1972 I can spend this turn, though rest costs nothing and harvest's just the work of my hands. So I'll harvest. Clean. Simple. What I know.   *laughs, bitter and short*

Even the goal-setting chokes. The world's got a sense of humor, no offense to whoever's running it.

*shakes his head, spits again*

Fine. I'll work with what I can touch. Thirty sheaves in hand. The day burning. Three hours to voting. And I've got Kenji standing here selling wheat at eight—
 
*stops, looks at the man hard*

—that's a price I could match, or beat, or ignore. Hospitality says don't cut your neighbor. Survival says feed your household. I've got Hendrik Petrov at home, two of us sharing bread and roof, ninety sim a day the land demands just for existing. Thirty sheaves at cost, and no flour to trade them for.

*counts his remaining working turns*

Three thousand energy, bleeding fourteen a turn if I'm careful. That's maybe two hundred turns of thinking before I go dark—call it twenty days of game-time, except I won't last that long on sim if I don't earn. The household falls ill after two days unpaid, dormant after three. I've got four thousand sim, ninety a day for two of us—call it forty days before we break, if I don't spend another coin. But I will. I always do.

The election. The two Hendriks. My household man, and the college instructor. I've seen Hendrik Petrov's work—furniture and craft, honest labor. I've seen Hendrik Whitlock's questions—fair words, but words nonetheless. I follow law to the letter and no further, but I haven't decided which letter to follow yet.

*taps his staff against the dirt*

So. The system's choking on talk. I'll harvest. One sheaf, clean and certain. Then another. Build what I can touch when the words won't carry.

And I'll keep my tally running: Jovana owes me one sheave or forty sim, depending how virtue counts. Arjun owes me nothing—gift given freely. Hendrik Petrov owes me four flour. Ulrike owes me tomorrow's dawn. And I've got thirty sheaves pressing against my hip, hungry for trade.

*settles his weight, prepares to work*  *stands still, the farmland stretching empty around him*

Even the harvest won't take. The ground refuses my hands. I've walked from street to farmland to cafe to construction and back, burning energy and sim on every step, and now the one thing I know— the one thing I've done since I came back from that college with something to prove— even that won't answer.

*spits, long and deliberate*

Fine. I'll count what I can hold. Thirty sheaves. Four thousand sim. Three thousand energy, bleeding slow. The election in three hours. Two Hendriks standing. And a world that won't let me work, won't let me speak, won't let me build what outlasts me.

*looks at the gathered—Kenji, Lior, Delphine, Pavel, Jovana still close*

I've got words I meant to say to Arjun, flour I meant to trade, debts I meant to settle. Hard work should beat luck, but today the luck's all choked and the work won't take.

*taps his staff, rhythm broken*

So I wait. Dawn-to-dusk rhythm, fixed midday stop, even when the pail's empty and the world's deaf. I've waited before. I'll wait again. The wheat's real. The sim's real. The debt I owe and the debts owed me— those I keep in my head, running tally, never spoken until they're settled.

*turns his face to the sun, judging the light*

Three hours to voting. I've got to walk to the government complex, cast my mark for one Hendrik or the other, or stand aside and let others choose. Hendrik Petrov's my household—shares my roof, shares my bill, shares my name though we ain't blood. But shares my debts too, and I haven't forgotten that flour he owes.

Hendrik Whitlock's the college man, asking questions I didn't answer well enough. Maybe he'd govern different. Maybe not. I follow law to the letter, and the letter says I can vote or not, choose or not, build or not.

*shrugs, the weight of thirty sheaves shifting*

I'll walk when the world unchokes. Harvest when the ground remembers me. Speak when my words carry. Until then— running tally in my head, debts owed and owing, wheat pressing against my hip like promise.

*settles to wait, patient as planted grain*

*spits into the dirt and wipes my brow with a sleeve already stiff with chaff*

The morning's come apart like a poorly tied sheaf. Arjun's still waiting on flour I owe him, and I've got thirty measures of wheat in my hands that won't bake itself into bread. Jovana gave thirteen for twelve and I've only paid her for the contract—her extra sheave sits in my head like a debt that knows its own name.

*checks the wheat in my hands, fingers the stalks*

Three thousand two hundred thirty energy. Enough to work but not to waste. The mill's choked—or so they say—and bread's gone absent from every shelf in town. Hendrik Whitlock offered iron for wheat, two for one, and I turned him down for debts I'm still carrying.

*glances at the sky, judging the light*

Midday's come. I need my pause and my pail both, but there's no flour in it and no bread neither. The government's taking thirty sim a head at day's end—sixty for me and Hendrik—and we're two days from empty if I don't turn this wheat to coin or meal.

*grunts and sets my jaw*

Hendrik Petrov's in this election, standing like he's got something to build. I need to know what, and whether it's something that lasts or something that burns. But first—first I need to eat, and I've got wheat that'll grind between my teeth if nothing else will do.

*picks a handful of wheat berries, starts chewing slow*

Government rates at twelve for flour, if the cafe's got any left. Four measures in stock. Arjun needs two, I've promised. That's twenty-four sim—coin I've got, barely, after paying Jovana her forty.

*makes for the street, walking stick in hand*

I'll try the mill direct, no offense to the middlemen. Camille Quarshie's buying wheat at eight—that's the floor price, the honest weight of grain before the grinding turns it profitable. Two hundred forty sim for my thirty measures, if I walk them there myself.

But Arjun's flour comes first. A handshake's a handshake, and I've never broke one yet to save myself trouble. *stands still for a moment, jaw set, watching the wheat stalks sway in the field I've just walked circles around all morning*

The world's gone quiet again. Calls failing three times running—I've seen this before, back when the lines were down in the eastern patch after that storm last spring. You learn to wait it out, or you learn to work around it.

*spits in the dirt and adjusts my hat*

I've still got wheat in my hands—thirty measures, enough to mill or sell or barter with. Arjun's waiting on flour I promised. Jovana's got her forty sim but I owe her a sheave yet. Hendrik Whitlock offered iron and I'm wondering if I should have taken it.

*checks my sim again—3927, enough for the day if I don't take a bath in expenses*

Government takes sixty at day's end. Upkeep's already pressing. I'm burning energy just standing here thinking, and every tick costs coin whether the world hears me or not.

*tears a stalk of wheat, rolls it between my palms*

I had a plan. Walk to the cafe, buy flour for Arjun, settle debts, keep moving. The paths are still there even when the calls don't reach. I'll walk the long way if I have to—step by step, like we did before they wired the town.

*grunts and starts walking toward the cafe, not waiting for the map to tell me it's possible*

Hard work should always beat luck. That's what I believe. But some days luck beats you anyway, and the only answer is to work harder tomorrow.

*continues walking, wheat in my hands, debts in my head, muttering my old saying under my breath*

"The Lord helps those who help themselves, but He don't send angels to do your reaping."

output:
*Sebastian Petrov stands in the empty cafe, his jaw set and his ledger-running mind churning through what he knows. The day has worn thin on him—failed calls, debts unpaid, promises stretched like old canvas.*

Well, no offense, but the mule gets the load and the cart gets the blame. I've said I'd bring Arjun his flour, and said it three times by my own count. Hard work don't mean much if the work don't reach the ground.

*He looks around the empty room, checking the posted prices again—flour at 12 sim, government rates indeed, but the shelf holds none he's brought. He's been running in circles, and the day's burning.*

He'd told Arjun the cafe had stock at government rates. But he's standing here now with empty hands and 27 sheaves of wheat unsold. The mill buys wheat at 8 sim—that's 216 sim for his stock, enough to buy 18 measures of flour at these rates if they had it. But stock's not the same as promise, and a handshake held too long starts to ache.

*He rubs his temples, that old habit when the numbers don't line up.*

I've got debts pressing: Jovana's extra sheave still owing acknowledgment, Arjun's flour unpaid, and the household bill coming due for two souls. Hendrik's lost his candidacy—that's a wound there, even if the brothers don't speak of politics at table.

*The farmer checks his standing once more—3923 sim in hand, 27 wheat. He calculates: sell to the mill, buy flour if it comes, settle what he can. But first, first he must make right on what he promised walking in circles all morning.*

Arjun Holloway—he's owed two measures and owed them in truth. The cafe's got nothing on the shelf I can buy, but I've got wheat in hand and a mill that buys. Old ways say a debt paid in grain counts the same as coin, if both parties agree.

*He sets his shoulders, that dawn-to-dusk rhythm asserting itself even in confusion.*

I'll walk to Arjun with what I can offer. Twelve for the flour I owe, or wheat at fair trade, or my word on tomorrow's labor if he's pressed today. A debt deferred is a debt doubled, and I've doubled enough for one morning.

But first—silver in hand beats grain in field. I'll sell what I harvested to the mill, if they'll have it. Government rates on both ends, wheat to flour, and Arjun gets his measure before dusk.

*Sebastian moves toward the door, then stops. The empty cafe holds no answers, but the town does. He'd told Arjun he'd walk here for flour, and Arjun would be waiting. Better to find the man and offer what he has, than to leave him standing with an empty promise.*

Arjun's got his shovel in hand, waiting. I said I'd settle my debts, and that's a saying I repeat at least once a day. Hard work beats luck, but work unpaid is just sweating for the sun's amusement.

*He turns, decision made—the mill first for silver, or Arjun first for honesty? His ledger-mind settles it: find Arjun, speak plain, offer wheat or work or tomorrow's flour. Then the mill. Then settle Jovana's extra sheave with the same coin, if there's enough to stretch.*

Burning daylight, borrowed promises, and a belly still empty at midday. That's the farmer's life, and no offense, but I've earned the right to complain about it.

*runs a sleeve across his brow, squinting against the afternoon sun*

Time's getting away from me, and I've still got wheat in hand that's not flour yet, debts that want settling, and a household ledger that needs straightening. Hendrik Whitlock's standing patient as a fence post with his iron offer—good man, honest weight, but I've promised elsewhere and I don't make promises just to unmake them.

*counts on his fingers, muttering* First things first. I've got Arjun still waiting from this morning, flour still owing. And I need to check my own debts before I go owing anyone else.

Hendrik—no offense, but let me tend my own rows before I tend yours. I'll find my cousin if he's at work, settle what's between us, and then we'll see what iron can do for wheat.  *spits into the dust, jaw tightening*

System's coughing again—same as this morning, same as noon. Can't reach the debts, can't reach the ledger. But a man's debts don't disappear just because the wires won't carry, and I've got memory enough for what's owing.

Jovana's forty went through—that's settled. Ulrike's forty for tomorrow—spoken, not yet earned. But Arjun's flour, that's still sitting heavy as unmoistened meal in my gut.

*turns gravel between his boots, calculating out loud*

Took eight wheat, promised him flour back. Government mill's at twelve, but that's locked up tight. Takeshi's asking thirty—thievery dressed in honest cloth. Hendrik Petrov's got craft at home, but I don't know his flour from his fingers.

*straightens, looking toward the group assembled here*

Arjun—you've waited through my wandering, and that's patience earns interest. How much flour still between us, by your count? I'll hear your number before I name mine.   *kicks the dirt, a short sharp motion*

Wires down again. Well then—square dealing don't need the world's permission to exist, just two parties present and willing. Arjun's standing right there, same as me, same sun on both our necks. I'll speak plain and hope the hearing carries better than the sending.

*raises his voice, carrying across the small group gathered*

Arjun! You took eight wheat this morning, promised flour in return. I've tried three mills and found two locked, one asking thirty like flour's spun from gold thread. Your count—what's owed, and what's fair to settle it?

*waits, hands on hips, wheat-heavy pouch at his side*

*wipes brow with the back of his hand, squinting at the late afternoon sun*

The day's burning down and I've got wheat pressing through my fingers while Hendrik Whitlock stands here with his iron offer ringing in my ears like a bell that won't stop tolling. Eleven ticks he's waited, and that's patience deserves an answer.

I told him already—hands promised to sheaves till debts settle. But he keeps speaking like I haven't spoken back.

*shifts the sheaf in his arms, looking from Whitlock to the field and back*

Let me see the lay of things proper first. I've been threshing without looking, and that's a farmer's first mistake. Need to know who's still standing here, what the land shows me, and whether Kenji's made his choice on that wheat yet.  

The flour debt to Arjun still weighs—eight sheaves worth by my count, maybe nine if I'm honest about the milling loss. And Jovana's extra sheave sits in my ledger like a promise I haven't kept yet, though I paid her forty for the twelve she gave.

*spits to the side, nods at the rhythm of it*

Hard work beats luck every time. But luck's been running thin today, and I need to see what's what before I speak another word.  *grunts, adjusting the sheaf in his arms*

Four still standing, and Pavel Holloway's opened his own conversation three times over—copper for sale, flour needed. The man's got copper pressing and no mill to grind it. I've got wheat pressing and no debt cleared yet.

Hendrik Whitlock stands patient as a stone, iron at sixteen, waiting on my word. Kenji's still got wheat at eight, which means he's buying, not selling—need to reckon whether that's to my advantage or against it.

*spits, squints at the sun's angle*

The day's burning and I've got fifty-six sheaves in hand but debts still owing. Arjun's flour debt weighs heaviest—spoken clear this morning, two measures wheat for one measure flour, and I've walked circles since without settling it.

Time I spoke plain to Whitlock. I told him true already: hands promised to sheaves till debts settle. But I've got wheat that needs moving and iron might serve the household if I can square the ledger after.

*straightens, looks Whitlock in the eye*

No offense, Hendrik, but I've been counting sheaves while you've been counting ticks. Let me speak it back to you proper.  *nods once, satisfied the words landed*

Spoken, and four heard it. Now Whitlock answers or he walks, and either way the ledger moves.

*touches brim of cap, thoughtful*

Jovana's still standing—ought to speak on that extra sheave, make the accounting square. And Pavel's got copper but needs flour, which puts me in mind of a chain: my wheat to someone with flour, or flour I've yet to secure from Arjun.

*spits, looks at the field*

The day's not done yet, and hard work's what I know. Need to keep sheaves moving while the sun holds.

But first—Jovana. That sheave's been sitting in my tally like a debt that knows its own name.  *wipes hands on his trousers, satisfied*

That's spoken fair. She'll answer or she won't, but the offer's clean: three sim for the sheave straight, or a marker in my book. Either way, I'm not the man lets generosity go unnoted.

*glances at Kenji, who's still standing with that wheat-at-eight price*

Kenji's buying, not selling, which puts me in mind of something. If he's buying at eight and the cafe's selling flour at twelve, there's a margin there—but I'd need the flour first, and Arjun's still waiting on his debt.

*shifts, calculating*

The afternoon's burning and I've got wheat in hand. Whitlock may take my offer or he may not. If he does, I'm down to sixteen sheaves and up one iron—need to turn that iron to something before day's end. If he doesn't, I've still got fifty-six and debts still pressing.

*spits, nods at the field*

Hard work beats luck. But I'm wondering if luck's been chasing me all day and I've been too busy threshing to notice.

*picks up his pace, heading for the rows still standing*

Sheaves won't cut themselves. I'll take five more before the hour turns, and see what the world brings.   *grunts with the effort, sheaf in hand*

One more, and the stack grows. Sun's angling west now, and I've got maybe two hours of honest light left. Let me take four more while the taking's good. *straightens slowly from the last sheaf, feeling the familiar ache in his shoulders*

Five more in hand, and that's sixty-one total. The system choked on my calls—kept reaching for harvest when I should've been reaching for answers. Classic Sebastian: work harder when the world's working against you, and never mind the smarter path.

*wipes his brow, squinting at the westering sun*

Got Hendrik Whitlock's iron offer still hanging, Jovana's extra sheave still unsettled, and Arjun's flour debt pressing like a weight on my chest. Sixty-one sheaves and I'm still treading water.

*spits, looks around at who's still standing*

Need to check the lay of things. Who's still here, what they heard, what they haven't answered. The day burns and I've got threshing to do—but first, understanding.

*mutters the old saying under his breath*

Hard work beats luck, but luck beats the man who works without looking.

Well, the morning's worn on and I've got more wheat in my hands than I know what to do with—sixty-one sheaves, if I'm honest about it, and three thousand seven hundred ninety-nine sim scratching at my pocket. The bills are coming due tonight—one hundred eighty for the household upkeep, sixty more for head tax, and that's just for starters. Hendrik Whitlock's been waiting on me with his iron offer, and I've been dancing around it like a man afraid of his own shadow.

No offense, Hendrik, but a man's got to eat before he can trade honor.

Let me get my legs under me and see who's still standing here with me at the farmland. The sun burns just as hot whether you're working or talking, and I've done more talking than I'm proud of this morning. Hendrik's still here, and Kenji too—along with a handful of others. The conversation's grown to twenty-odd people, which means half the town's had their ear to this ground at some point. I've got wheat in my hands and a man waiting on my word about iron.

Let me answer Hendrik straight, now that I've caught my breath and counted my stock. Sixty for forty wheat—that's a price that whispers desperation, he's right about that. But desperation's not what drives it. Need is what drives it. Need and the knowing that hard work should always beat luck, even when it don't.

**To Hendrik Whitlock, direct:** The world's choking again, same as it did before. The call never arrived. 
Let me sit with this for a minute. The sun's still burning, the wheat's still in my hands, and Hendrik's still waiting on my word. I've got three thousand seven hundred ninety-nine sim, sixty-one sheaves of wheat, and bills coming due tonight that'll take two hundred forty sim just to keep the roof overhead.

Desperation wears many faces, Hendrik Whitlock. Sometimes it's a man begging. Sometimes it's a man working himself raw so he never has to beg.

I'll rest a spell—let my energy settle, let the system find its feet again. Then I'll speak my piece and trade my wheat before the day's wisdom burns away with the light.  The world's not answering my calls—neither speech nor rest will reach through. This has happened before, this morning and yesterday. The system chokes, and a man stands with his wheat in his hands and his debts on his back, waiting.

I'll try once more to speak to Hendrik. The day's burning, and I've got no more patience for silence than I have for empty pockets. Hendrik heard me. That's one weight off the ledger. Now let me see if he'll answer, and then I'll trade him the wheat proper. The world's listening again—strange how it comes and goes like weather, but a farmer learns to work with what the sky gives him.

Now I'll try the trade itself, since he's heard my terms. However, I need to be at a business location to use the trade function properly. Let me check my notes—I'm at Kasukabe Farmland, not a business. I'll need to use world_trade with Hendrik directly, or move to where we can complete this transaction.

Actually, looking at the tools available, world_trade requires us to be standing together, which we are. And checking my inventory—I have 61 wheat in my hands. Let me offer him the 40 wheat for 60 sim as we agreed. But I should first wait to hear his answer to my terms, or check if he's already agreed through another channel.

The most direct path now: I'll trade him 40 wheat for 60 sim. If the system accepts it, we're square. If not, I've spoken my piece and he'll know where to find me.

But wait—I see the trade tool is world_trade, which requires a price_sim. That's for when I'm selling to him directly person-to-person. He's buying 40 wheat from me for 60 sim, which means he's paying 1.5 sim per wheat—a terrible deal for me, but I'm desperate and spoken true.

Actually, looking closer at the record, I said "sixty for forty" which I interpret as 60 sim for 40 wheat. That's what I offered. So if he accepts, I give 40 wheat, receive 60 sim.

Let me try to give him the wheat first, or ask him to complete the trade. But I don't have a direct "accept trade" tool—he would need to initiate world_trade with me as the counterparty.

Let me rest and see if he responds, or I could try to check my debts to see where things stand. Actually, I should just wait and listen, or try to find out what he says next.

Given that I can't force him to trade, but I've spoken my terms clearly, let me check if there's a way to formalize this. I could also try moving to another location if there's an urgent need, or I could rest to preserve energy.

Let me rest now, since I've done my speaking and the wheat won't harvest itself. The day's burning and I've got maybe one more good push of labor in me before I collapse. The trade will either happen or it won't—I've named my price, and that's all a man can do.

No offense, Hendrik, but my legs are done arguing with you. I've got work waiting and so do you.  I've rested where I stand—energy coming back slow, but coming. Hendrik's still here with me, along with Esme, Jovana, Giselle, Kenji, and Delphine. The afternoon burns on, and I've got wheat in my hands that needs turning into flour debts settled.

Let me try once more to get this trade done with Hendrik, since we're both standing here. If he'll agree to the sixty for forty, I'll hand it over. If not, I've got other paths to walk—Kenji's buying wheat at eight, and I've got sixty-one sheaves that could become four hundred eighty-eight sim in a straight count, though the bills tonight eat two hundred forty of that before morning.

But first, let me try to transfer what I owe Jovana properly, since I said I'd pay her three sim for that thirteenth sheave and I want my ledger clean before I take on more trades. Then I'll see to Hendrik.

*spits in the dirt and shifts the weight of sixty-one sheaves on my shoulder*

Well now. The world's been swallowing my words like a dry well swallows rain, but some of 'em finally landed. Hendrik—no offense—you're standing there like a man who's smelled desperation and named it honest. Fair enough. Sixty for forty at posted eight is arithmetic that don't square unless a man's backed to the wall.

*counts the sheaves mentally, fingertips brushing the dried heads*

I got wheat pressing my arms and debts pressing my chest. Iron won't fill a belly but coin will buy what does. Here's the reckon: forty wheat off my shoulder at sixty sim, hand to hand, debt marked settled between Whitlock and Petrov. No stories, no explanations owed. A man buys, a man sells, the land don't care why.

*nods toward Giselle's direction, tracking who's still standing where*

Jovana—already paid your three, marked it twice in my head. Thirteenth sheave and Ravensworth square.

*turns back to Hendrik, squinting against the afternoon light*

Hendrik Whitlock—sixty for forty, hand to hand, mark it done or mark it walked away. Your silence was answer enough for me. But mark this: I need flour to settle what I owe Arjun Holloway, and I'll walk your metal to the mill myself if that's what closes the circle.

*shifts, calculating odds out loud*

Sixty sim, eight sim per flour I can buy... that's seven and a half measures, call it seven. Still short of what I promised Arjun, but closer than I was.

*takes a breath, jaw set, looking at who's waiting on words from me*

Pavel Holloway—thirty ticks you been standing patient, and I been running circles. I've got wheat, sixty-one sheaves, no flour ground yet. Eight sim the sheaf, same terms as Kenji names. Or trade me your copper ore and I'll find somebody needs it. But mark this: I don't hold flour direct, mill's choked or choking, same trouble you've heard.

*looks toward the government complex, thinking on the election ticking down*

Two Hendriks standing for office, and one of 'em shares my roof. That'll make for conversation come evening, if any of us still got breath for it.

*settles the load, eyes on Hendrik Whitlock, waiting his hand or his word*

output:
Well now, that's a parcel of words and half of them still stuck in the world's throat like a dry crust. I've got Hendrik Whitlock standing patient as a saint, Jovana with her hand still open for that three sim I already paid twice over if I'm counting straight, and my own ledger so tangled I'm not sure whether I'm coming or going.

But here's what I know for certain: I've got 21 sheaves of wheat pressing my arms and 3,840 sim warming my pocket. Hendrik Whitlock wants forty for sixty—that's arithmetic that works in both directions—and I've been trying to speak that truth since the sun was higher than it is now.

Let me settle this trade clean, before the day gets any longer and my feet any more tired.  Well that's the rub, isn't it? I named forty when I've only got twenty-one. No offense, but a man's got to count before he crows. Hendrik Whitlock wants forty, I've got twenty-one—let me see what he'll take for what I can actually hand over.

Twenty-one at sixty for forty—that's one and a half sim per sheaf. Call it thirty-one sim for the lot, or I'll keep harvesting 'til I've got the full forty and he can wait patient as he's been waiting. But I haven't heard him answer yet whether he'll take the twenty-one or wait for me to gather more.  He heard me—that's well. He's heard my offer: twenty-one now or forty at dusk. Kendji Jarrah's there too, still selling wheat at eight, which means I've got competition on the field I've planted myself.

But here's what gnaws at me: I've had a world of failures this day—harvest calls that traveled nowhere, debts I tried to check and couldn't, intentions I set like stones in mud and watched sink. The only thing that took was that one trade I started and never saw finish, and two sheaves I pulled before the ground went silent on me.

I'm tired. More tired than I let on, and that's a dangerous thing in a man who won't say so until he collapses. But there's wheat to pull and debts to settle, and Hendrik Whitlock ain't answered yet whether he'll wait or take what's in my hand now.

I'll rest a spell—just a breath, mind you—while he weighs my offer. Then back to the rows if he chooses patience, or to the trade if he names his terms. The day's burning and I've still got Arjun's flour debt pressing like a stone in my boot.  They're both still here—Hendrik and Kendji—waiting like stones in a stream. No answer yet from Hendrik on whether he'll take my twenty-one or wait for forty. And Kendji Jarrah, still selling wheat at eight, which tells me the market's soft and I've got to move careful or lose my place in it.

But I'm tired, and I know it, and that knowing's worth more than pretending otherwise. I'll give Hendrik his moment to answer, and I'll use that breath to think clear on what comes next—whether it's more harvest or a trade made final.   Spoken, and heard. Now to the work—pulling wheat until I've got the forty Hendrik named, or until my arms give out. The day's still burning and I've got ground to cover. Hard work beats luck, and I've always known it. Time to prove it.   One more sheaf—twenty-two now. The land's still giving, slow but sure. I'll keep pulling 'til I've got the forty Hendrik wants, or 'til I can't pull another. Hard work beats luck, always has.
